title: They Said Romance Was Dead. Cocktail 2 Just Poured Itself ₹130 Crore.
excerpt: Shahid Kapoor, Kriti Sanon, and Rashmika Mandanna's sun-drenched sequel has crossed ₹100 crore domestically in 11 days — surpassing the original and proving that in 2026, love still sells.
body:
There's something almost embarrassingly romantic about this victory.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=XXxUqLHq1xg</youtube>

In a year when **Bollywood** has been drunk on horror, high on franchise blood, and unapologetically chasing the youngest, darkest impulses in the multiplex, a love story just walked in wearing heels and ordered the most expensive thing on the menu.

**Cocktail 2** — **Homi Adajania**'s sun-soaked, messy, gloriously attractive sequel — crossed **₹100 crore at the domestic box office** on Monday, its eleventh day in theatres. The worldwide gross stands at a breathtaking **₹130 crore**, comfortably surpassing the original **Cocktail**'s lifetime total of ₹121 crore. It is now the fourth Bollywood film of 2026 to breach the century mark domestically, joining **Bhooth Bangla**, **Dhurandhar 2**, and **Border 2** — three films that could not be further from a love triangle if they tried.

And yet here we are. Romance isn't just alive. It's wearing a backless dress and turning heads.

**Shahid Kapoor** needed this one badly. His last outing, **O Romeo** in February, opened to a limp ₹8.5 crore and disappeared before anyone could learn the songs. The whispers had started — that he'd lost the plot, that the audience had moved on, that post-**Kabir Singh** Shahid was a diminishing asset. Cocktail 2 has incinerated that narrative. His opening day of ₹13.5 crore was the kind of entrance that silences a room. By Sunday, the first weekend had stacked up to ₹46.76 crore, and the weekdays held with the stubbornness of a man who knows he's winning.



What makes the numbers more impressive is the company he's keeping. **Kriti Sanon**, who plays the sharp, funny, slightly dangerous third vertex of this triangle, just delivered her second-highest post-pandemic opener, overtaking even **Crew**. And **Rashmika Mandanna**, already a certified pan-India draw after the **Pushpa** franchise, brings a warmth and vulnerability that balances the film's wilder instincts. The three of them together have a chemistry that doesn't feel manufactured — it feels *found*.



> "We didn't set out to make a sequel. We set out to make a film about people who make beautiful mistakes." — Homi Adajania

The original **Cocktail** arrived in 2012 with **Saif Ali Khan**, **Deepika Padukone**, and **Diana Penty**, and it did something rare: it made a love triangle feel modern, urban, and a little bit dangerous. The soundtrack — *Tumhi Ho Bandhu*, *Angreji Beat* — became the playlist of a generation. It grossed ₹121 crore worldwide on a ₹35 crore budget, and for years, fans begged for a sequel that never came.

Fourteen years later, the sequel doesn't try to recreate that magic. It builds something new — different leads, different energy, same emotional recklessness.

The critical reception has been polarised, which is exactly what a good Cocktail should be. Some reviewers called it indulgent. Others called it the most watchable Hindi film of the year. What nobody called it was boring. The fashion alone — Kriti in structured blazers and nothing underneath, Rashmika in florals that somehow feel threatening, Shahid in the kind of casual menswear that makes you rethink your entire wardrobe — has generated its own discourse.

**For diaspora audiences**, the math is simple: this is a glossy, good-looking, well-soundtracked date night film in a season starved of them. It's the kind of movie you take someone to when you want to hold hands in the dark and not think about geopolitics for two hours. The soundtrack is streaming everywhere, and if you're in the US, UK, or Canada, check your local IMAX and PVR screenings — it's still running strong in overseas markets, where it's already crossed ₹28 crore.

The bigger story here is industrial. Bollywood's 2026 first half has been dominated by horror (**Bhooth Bangla**), action (**Border 2**), and comedy-action hybrids (**Welcome to the Jungle**). The rom-com — once the bread and butter of the Hindi film industry — has been treated as a dying genre, too soft for the era of ₹500-crore tentpoles. Cocktail 2 just proved that when you cast it right, style it right, and give the audience permission to feel something, love still fills theatres.

Four films at ₹100 crore in six months. And the one that feels most alive? The one about three people who can't stop making terrible romantic decisions.
